summary: Xipamide is a sulfonamide thiazide-like diuretic used for hypertension and oedema. The usual dose is 20 mg once daily in the morning for hypertension (up to 40 mg) and 40 mg daily for oedema (reducing to 20 mg, maximum 80 mg). It inhibits sodium chloride reabsorption in the early distal tubule, producing natriuresis and diuresis with potassium loss. It is not FDA-approved; dosing here follows the EMA/SmPC and BNF. Monitor potassium, sodium, renal function and uric acid.
indications: Essential hypertension (alone or with other antihypertensives)
Oedema, including that associated with cardiac, hepatic or renal disease

dosage.d: 20 mg once daily in the morning; increase to 40 mg once daily if required
dosage.n: Lowest effective dose; combine with other agents if needed

dosage.d: 40 mg once daily in the morning, reduced gradually to maintenance 20 mg according to response
dosage.n: Maximum 80 mg daily in resistant oedema

dosage.d: Start at the lower end of the range; titrate to response
dosage.n: Greater risk of electrolyte disturbance and hypotension

admin: Take as a single dose in the morning to avoid nocturnal diuresis
Swallow tablets whole with water, with or after food
Use the lowest effective dose and titrate to clinical response
Correct hypokalemia and other electrolyte disturbances before and during therapy
Combine with potassium-sparing agents or supplements if hypokalemia is a concern
moa: Xipamide is a sulfonamide diuretic structurally related to the thiazides. It inhibits sodium and chloride reabsorption in the early (cortical) distal renal tubule, producing chloruresis and natriuresis with secondary osmotic water loss. Increased distal tubular flow stimulates potassium secretion (kaliuresis); calcium, magnesium and bicarbonate excretion also rise acutely. Unlike thiazides, it appears to act partly from the peritubular (blood) side. The resulting volume reduction and, with chronic use, reduced peripheral vascular resistance lower blood pressure.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to xipamide or other sulfonamides

preg: Xipamide is not recommended in pregnancy. Thiazide-type diuretics can reduce placental perfusion and cause fetal/neonatal electrolyte disturbance, thrombocytopenia and jaundice; use only if there is no safer alternative.
lact: Xipamide passes into breast milk and may suppress lactation. Breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment.
renal: Contraindicated in anuria and severe renal failure, where it is ineffective and risks worsening azotemia. Use cautiously in lesser impairment with monitoring of electrolytes and renal function; about one third of the dose is excreted unchanged renally.
hepatic: Contraindicated in hepatic precoma and coma because diuretic-induced electrolyte shifts (hypokalemia, alkalosis) can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. Use cautiously in lesser hepatic impairment.

major: Lithium - reduced renal clearance and increased lithium toxicity
Class III antiarrhythmics and other QT-prolonging drugs - hypokalemia increases risk of torsades
Digoxin/cardiac glycosides - hypokalemia potentiates glycoside toxicity
moderate: Other antihypertensives - additive blood-pressure lowering / first-dose hypotension
Corticosteroids, amphotericin B, other diuretics - additive potassium loss
NSAIDs - reduced diuretic and antihypertensive effect, risk of renal impairment
minor: Calcium salts / vitamin D - risk of hypercalcemia
Curare-type muscle relaxants - enhanced effect with hypokalemia
interactions.food: May be taken with or after food; high salt intake reduces antihypertensive effect.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid excessive alcohol - increases risk of orthostatic hypotension.
interactions.diagnostics: May raise blood glucose, uric acid, urea and creatinine; may lower serum potassium and sodium; can reduce protein-bound iodine without thyroid dysfunction.

common: Hypokalemia (may cause nausea, muscle weakness or cramps, ECG changes)
Increased urea, uric acid and creatinine initially
emergency: Severe hyponatremia/hypokalemia with arrhythmia or seizures

monitoring: Serum potassium and sodium, especially early and in the elderly
Serum uric acid in patients prone to gout
Blood pressure and signs of volume depletion
counsel: Take the dose in the morning to avoid needing to pass urine at night
Report muscle cramps, weakness, severe tiredness, confusion or palpitations (possible electrolyte imbalance)
Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness, especially when starting treatment
Eat potassium-rich foods if advised, and report gout symptoms
Avoid excess alcohol and tell your doctor if you have diabetes or gout
pk: Store at room temperature, protected from moisture (per SmPC)
pearls: Not FDA-approved; dosing and labeling here follow EMA/SmPC (Aquaphor/Aquaphoril) and the BNF
Thiazide-like but partly acts from the peritubular (blood) side; useful even at moderately reduced GFR
Hypokalemia is common (>10%) - monitor potassium and consider supplementation or a potassium-sparing agent
Sulfonamide structure - avoid in sulfonamide allergy and watch for acute angle-closure glaucoma
Can precipitate gout; check uric acid in predisposed patients
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember in the morning. If it is late in the day or almost time for the next day's dose, skip it (to avoid nighttime diuresis) and continue the normal schedule. Do not take a double dose.
overdose: Overdose causes excessive diuresis with dehydration, hypovolemia, hypotension and electrolyte disturbances (hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis), which may cause arrhythmias, weakness and confusion. There is no specific antidote. Treat by stopping the drug, restoring fluid and electrolyte balance and providing supportive care.
